Researchers count giant tortoises on a remote island

A survey team spent three months walking transects across the island, marking every tortoise they found and estimating the population from repeat sightings. The count came in far higher than earlier estimates, which relied on aerial photographs.

The researchers said the larger number reflects better methods rather than a sudden boom. Dense scrub hides many animals from the air, and ground surveys reach areas that were previously skipped.

Conservation groups welcomed the result but warned that invasive plants and rising temperatures still threaten nesting sites. They plan to repeat the survey every five years to track long-term trends.

Local rangers will use the new data to decide where to clear invasive species first, focusing on slopes where hatchlings were most often seen.
